title: Generics

notes: Inventory<T> is written once and works for any type.
new Inventory<string>(2) fixes T to string; adding an int would not compile.
where T : IComparable<T> is what makes x.CompareTo(best) allowed.
Largest works for ints and strings without any copying.

exercises.title: Generic helpers
exercises.prompt:
In static class Util write three generic methods:
- T Largest<T>(List<T> items) where T : IComparable<T>: the biggest item; an empty list throws InvalidOperationException.
- List<T> Repeat<T>(T item, int times): a list with the item that many times; negative times throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
- void Swap<T>(ref T a, ref T b): swaps the two variables.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { int a = 1, b = 2; Util.Swap(ref a, ref b); string x = "hi", y = "yo"; Util.Swap(ref x, ref y); return a + " " + b + " " + x + " " + y; }))()
tests.name: swap

tests.why: Largest needs the constraint where T : IComparable<T>.

hints: Largest: if (items.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("empty"); then keep the best so far with CompareTo.
public static List<T> Repeat<T>(T item, int times) { var list = new List<T>(); for (...) list.Add(item); return list; }
public static void Swap<T>(ref T a, ref T b) { T temp = a; a = b; b = temp; }

exercises.title: Inventory<T>
exercises.prompt:
Write class Inventory<T>:
- constructor Inventory(int capacity): capacity under 1 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Property Capacity.
- Count, IsFull (Count has reached Capacity).
- bool Add(T item): false (and nothing added) when full, else true.
- bool Remove(T item): removes one, true if it was there.
- an indexer T this[int index] (read only).
- List<T> ToList(): a COPY of the items, so changing it doesn't change the inventory.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var bag = new Inventory<string>(2); bool a = bag.Add("sword"); bool b = bag.Add("shield"); bool c = bag.Add("bow"); return a + " " + b + " " + c + " " + bag.Count + " " + bag.IsFull; }))()
tests.name: fills up

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var ammo = new Inventory<int>(5); ammo.Add(30); ammo.Add(12); ammo.Remove(30); return ammo[0] + " " + ammo.Count + " " + ammo.Capacity; }))()
tests.name: works with ints

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var bag = new Inventory<string>(3); bag.Add("potion"); var copy = bag.ToList(); copy.Add("cheat"); return bag.Count.ToString(); }))()
tests.name: ToList is a copy

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var bag = new Inventory<string>(2); return bag.Remove("ghost").ToString(); }))()
tests.name: removing something missing

hints: Keep a private readonly List<T> items = new(); inside.
public bool IsFull => items.Count >= Capacity;  public T this[int index] => items[index];

exercises.title: An object pool
exercises.prompt:
Write class Pool<T> where T : class, new() (the class Bullet is given to try it with):
- constructor Pool(int prewarm): creates that many objects up front (negative throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException).
- Created: how many objects the pool has made in total. Available: how many are waiting in the pool.
- T Get(): hands out a waiting object, or makes a new one if none are waiting.
- void Release(T item): puts it back. null throws ArgumentNullException; releasing an object that is already in the pool throws InvalidOperationException.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var pool = new Pool<Bullet>(3); return pool.Available + " " + pool.Created; }))()
tests.name: prewarm

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var pool = new Pool<Bullet>(1); var a = pool.Get(); var b = pool.Get(); return pool.Available + " " + pool.Created; }))()
tests.name: makes more when empty

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var pool = new Pool<Bullet>(0); var a = pool.Get(); pool.Release(a); var b = pool.Get(); return ReferenceEquals(a, b) + " " + pool.Created; }))()
tests.name: reuses released objects

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var pool = new Pool<Bullet>(0); var a = pool.Get(); pool.Release(a); pool.Release(a); return "no error"; }))()
tests.name: double release

hints: Keep the waiting objects in a private readonly Stack<T> free = new();
Get: if (free.Count > 0) return free.Pop(); Created++; return new T();
Release: if (free.Contains(item)) throw new InvalidOperationException(...); free.Push(item);

quiz.q: What does the T in Inventory<T> stand for?
choices: A type the user of the class chooses

quiz.q: var bag = new Inventory<string>(5); bag.Add(42); What happens?
quiz.why: Generics are checked by the compiler.

quiz.q: Why does Largest<T> need where T : IComparable<T>?
choices: Without it the compiler won't let you call CompareTo on a T
quiz.why: The constraint promises T can be compared.

quiz.q: Which constraint lets you write new T()?
Why do games pool bullets instead of creating new ones every shot?
choices: Making and throwing away many objects causes stutters; reuse is smoother
Pools use more memory on purpose

cards.a: public static List<T> Repeat<T>(T item, int times)
Keep used objects and hand them out again instead of creating new ones

explain: Explain what generics are for, using an example of code you would otherwise have to copy for each type.
